function_question: How does nature solve YOUR problem?

hero.name: Ellie
hero.role: a young inventor and your guide

opening.text: There was a young inventor called Ellie, who carried a notebook everywhere to write down things that could work better.
Ellie added a new problem to the list: a squeaky door, a leaky bottle, a bag strap that kept slipping.

A poster went up: "The Inventors' Fair! Bring a real problem and a nature-inspired solution." Ellie picked one straight away: their classroom got hot and stuffy every afternoon. "What problem will YOU pick?" they asked.

card.hero: You, 13+, with Ellie as your guide
card.problem: Your own real problem: pick one at school or home
card.goal: Run the full Biomimicry Design Spiral and pitch your invention
card.rules: A real problem, a fair test with a control, and your own success measure. Safe materials only.

guide.brief: I'm Popi, your story guide. This is the final mission, and the problem is yours to choose. Ellie will show you every step with their own problem. Can you solve yours with nature's help? Let's start!
guide.your_idea: Some inventors already have a problem and a spark of an idea. Do you?
guide.nature_clues: Every famous nature copy started with a function. Tap each card, then go and discover your own living thing!
guide.design_secret: Here's the secret every biomimicry designer knows…
guide.skill: Predict first: which verb describes what your design must DO? Try 3 different verbs before you search.
guide.sketch: Draw your invention and link it to nature's strategy with an arrow!
guide.build_and_test: Build your prototype and test it against a control, 3 times each. Numbers win pitches!
guide.retry_tip: Inventors never stop at round 1. Change ONE thing, run 3 more trials, and see if your average improves.
guide.ending: And ever since then, you've looked at every problem and asked: how would nature do this? Ellie's classroom stays cool too, thanks to a chimney idea borrowed from a prairie dog.

quick_check.question: The Eastgate Centre uses about 10% of the energy of a similar building for heating and cooling. If a normal building uses 500 units, about how many does Eastgate use?
quick_check.right: Right! 10% of 500 is 50. The other 450 units are saved by copying termites.
quick_check.wrong: Not quite. 10% means one tenth, so divide 500 by 10.

clue_cards.name: Prairie dog (Ellie's find)
clue_cards.trick: Burrow openings at two different heights.
clue_cards.does: Wind over the openings pulls fresh air through the tunnels. Now search AskNature for yours!

clue_cards.name: Kingfisher
clue_cards.does: It slips into water with barely a splash, and inspired a quieter bullet train.

clue_cards.name: Burdock
clue_cards.trick: Tiny hooks all over its burrs.
clue_cards.does: They catch on loops in fur, and inspired Velcro.

clue_cards.name: Termite mound
clue_cards.trick: Tunnels and chimneys that move air.
clue_cards.does: They stop the nest overheating, and inspired the Eastgate Centre.

predict.prompt: Copy the look or copy the strategy? Predict which one really works!

items.label: A drone painted with feather patterns
A train nose shaped to part the air gradually
A building with chimneys that pull air through

predict.explain: Biomimicry copies HOW nature works, not how it looks. Painted feathers change nothing, but a shape or an airflow trick can save real energy.

lab.title: Ellie's shoebox classroom lab
lab.predict: Four shoebox classrooms sit in the same sunny window for 20 minutes. Which will stay coolest inside?
options: A low vent + a tall chimney
A low vent + a tall black chimney

tool.name: Biomimicry Design Spiral
tool.intro: You've met these steps in earlier missions. The Biomimicry Design Spiral puts all 6 together, the way professional designers use them. Today you'll run the whole spiral on your own problem.
tool.example_object: an umbrella that flips inside out

parts.name: Define
parts.what: Say what your design must DO, for whom, and how you'll measure success.
parts.example: ☂️ It must stay open in gusts of wind, tested in front of a fan.
parts.starter: My design must… and I'll measure success by…

parts.name: Biologize
parts.what: Turn the function into a nature question.
parts.example: ☂️ How does nature survive strong wind without breaking?

parts.name: Discover
parts.what: Find living things that do it well.
parts.example: ☂️ Palm trees bend in storms; bat wings flex and spring back.
parts.starter: Living things that do this: …, … and …

parts.name: Abstract
parts.what: Write the trick in plain words, without the animal.
parts.example: ☂️ Flexible parts that bend and spring back, plus gaps that let gusts through.

parts.name: Emulate
parts.what: Build your design using that principle.
parts.example: ☂️ A two-layer canopy with a vent, on bendy ribs.
parts.starter: My prototype copies the principle by…

parts.name: Evaluate
parts.what: Test against a control, then decide what to change.
parts.example: ☂️ In front of a fan, the normal umbrella flips and the vented one holds.
parts.starter: Compared with my control, my design… so next I'll…

sketch_checklist: I drew my invention with labels.
I linked it to a living thing's strategy with my design principle.
I wrote my success measure, my control and my one variable.

test.measure: your own success measure (how much better than the control)
test.check_question: Fair test check: how many trials did you run for your design and for your control?

reflection.question: Which nature inventor inspired you most?
options: 🐾 Prairie dog: air through the burrow
